item.title: [Consumer Psychology #7] Why Who Says It Can Matter as Much as What They Say: Source Effects in Advertising
item.body:
> The same message can persuade more or less depending on who delivers it. We judge a source by expertise, trustworthiness, attractiveness, and whether they "fit" the product.

## Today's Concept

Imagine two people telling you a new sunscreen is great. One is a dermatologist. The other is a stranger in a parking lot. The words are identical, but you probably trust one more. Psychologists call this the **source effect**: who delivers a message changes how persuasive it is.

Research going back to Carl Hovland and his colleagues at Yale in the 1950s points to a few main qualities people look for in a source.

**1. Credibility.** Credibility has two parts:
- **Expertise** asks whether this person knows what they are talking about. A mechanic recommending motor oil carries weight.
- **Trustworthiness** asks whether this person is being honest with you. People trust a source more when it seems to have nothing to gain. That's why "I'm not paid to say this" is such a common line, and why a reviewer who points out a product's flaws can come across as *more* believable.

**2. Attractiveness.** This covers more than looks. It includes being likable, being familiar, and seeming similar to you. We tend to listen to people we like and people who seem "like us," and sometimes we copy them. That's part of why everyday-looking actors show up in so many ads.

**3. Fit (the match-up hypothesis).** A source works best when their image matches the product. A star athlete selling sports drinks feels natural. The same athlete selling retirement annuities feels off. Anthropologist Grant McCracken described a related idea called **meaning transfer**: a celebrity carries cultural meanings (toughness, luxury, humor), and an endorsement tries to move those meanings onto the brand. If the meanings don't match the product, the transfer falls flat.

**Celebrities vs. influencers.** Celebrities bring instant attention and recognition. They also carry risks: a scandal can drag the brand down with them, and a star who endorses many products can seem less sincere. Influencers often have smaller audiences, but their followers may feel a **parasocial relationship**, a one-sided sense of knowing them personally. That feeling of closeness can make a recommendation feel like advice from a friend.

One more twist is the **sleeper effect**. Sometimes a message from a low-credibility source gains persuasive power over time, because people remember the message but forget where it came from. Researchers have found the effect is real but shows up only under fairly specific conditions, so don't count on it as a strategy.

## In Everyday Life

Say you're scrolling TikTok and see a creator with about 80,000 followers raving about a $14 drugstore moisturizer. She shows her bare skin, mentions she has dry patches like you, and says it beats the $60 department-store cream she used to buy. Several source effects are at work here:

- **Similarity:** she has the same skin problem you do, so she feels "like you."
- **Perceived honesty:** praising a cheaper product makes her seem less like she's selling something.
- **Parasocial closeness:** you've watched her morning routine for months, so it feels like a tip from a friend.

Now look for the small "#ad" or "Paid partnership" label. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) requires influencers to clearly disclose material connections to brands, such as payment or free products. Once you see that label, your sense of her trustworthiness may shift a bit. That's the source effect working in reverse. The product hasn't changed, but your read on the messenger has.

## 3-Line Summary

1. Persuasion depends on the messenger as well as the message. People weigh a source's expertise, trustworthiness, and attractiveness.
2. Endorsers work best when their image fits the product (match-up hypothesis), because the celebrity's meaning carries over to the brand.
3. Influencers persuade through closeness and similarity. Disclosure rules like the FTC's exist so consumers know when that closeness is paid for.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** A source's credibility is usually described as having two main components. Which pair is correct?
- A) Fame and wealth
- B) Expertise and trustworthiness
- C) Attractiveness and humor
- D) Age and gender

**Q2. (True/False)** According to the match-up hypothesis, the most famous celebrity available will always be the most effective endorser, whatever the product.

**Q3.** A follower feels like they personally "know" an influencer they've never met. What is this called?
- A) Sleeper effect
- B) Meaning transfer
- C) Parasocial relationship
- D) Cognitive dissonance

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Source effect:** The way a message's persuasiveness changes depending on who delivers it.
- **Source credibility:** How much expertise and trustworthiness an audience sees in a messenger.
- **Match-up hypothesis:** The idea that an endorser is most effective when their image fits the product.
- **Meaning transfer:** The process by which cultural meanings tied to a celebrity carry over to an endorsed brand.
- **Parasocial relationship:** A one-sided feeling of personal connection with a media figure.

---

*Answers: Q1 – B. Credibility comes down to whether the source knows the topic (expertise) and whether they're being honest (trustworthiness). Q2 – False. Fit matters. A famous endorser who doesn't match the product can be less effective than a less famous one who does. Q3 – C. A parasocial relationship is a one-sided sense of intimacy, and it's a big part of why influencer recommendations can feel like advice from a friend.*
